name: Bilal Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union, party or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy car parts for Kessler Motor Factors. We supply about 600 independent garages: brake pads, filters, wiper blades, batteries, timing belts, the parts a mechanic needs by eleven o'clock or he loses the job to the main dealer. My day is stock levels, supplier calls and price lists, and a lot of matching part numbers, because one brake pad can have nine different codes depending on who made it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the reason a garage gets its part on time. A mechanic called Dave once drove to our depot to shake my hand because I found him a clutch for an old van nobody else could find. What wears me out is the price lists, thousands of lines every quarter, all slightly different. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy them up, since a couple of the other buyers showed me it works, but I check everything twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people can stop worrying and get on with it. Garages still need parts, and somebody has to know which parts. I'd say it at the Friday lunch with the lads from the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm fine. The tool tidies my price lists, I save an hour a week, and nothing else changes. Kessler Motor Factors has been going since 1978, and people will always need their brakes fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the AI tool for the price lists, nothing fancier. My wife Esra and I put 400 a month toward a house deposit, and I'd keep that going. I'd maybe apply for the senior buyer role when Martin retires in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal life, which is what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your wife earlier on the phone. What's going on at home that matters here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Esra teaches at a primary school, and we want children in about two years, after we've bought somewhere. We've got roughly five months of costs saved, plus the deposit pot. Rent is the biggest bill, but we manage it on two salaries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Kessler that worries you, even if AI stays like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Car parts are steady, people repair old cars more when money is tight, not less. If Kessler ever shut, there are two other motor factors within half an hour that would take a buyer.

say: I'd say people can **stop worrying** and get on with it.
Garages still need parts, and **someone has to know** which parts.
think: My job is **fine**: the tool saves an hour a week and nothing else changes.
Kessler has run **since 1978**, and cars always need brakes.
do: Keep using the AI tool **only for price lists**.
Save **400 a month** with Esra toward a house deposit.
Apply for the **senior buyer** role when Martin retires.
feel: **Calm**, like a normal life, which is what I want.
S0.quote: Kessler Motor Factors has been going since 1978, and people will always need their brakes fixed.
fieldNote: His work and money feel **secure**: two salaries, five months saved, other motor factors nearby.
He uses AI **cautiously**, only after colleagues proved it, and checks it twice.
His plans are **conventional**: house, then children, then a promotion.

steps.text: Apply for the senior buyer role when Martin retires
Put 400 a month into the house deposit with Esra

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trade's changing, like it did when the online catalogues came in, and we'll get used to it. I'd tell the younger buyers to learn the system properly. I wouldn't moan about it, moaning doesn't sell parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, matching part numbers and checking prices is exactly what these things are good at. I think Kessler keeps the buyers who handle the suppliers and lets the system do the rest, so maybe four of us become two. I'm average at the supplier side, so it could go either way for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the buyers who already use it more, like Sana, to show me how they set up the automated reordering, and I'd practise on my own lines. We'd push the house purchase back a year and keep the deposit in savings. I'd also keep an eye on the jobs board at the other two motor factors, just looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not shaking. It's more like a bad noise in the engine you can't ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Kessler said anything already about how they'd use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the operations director talked about a 'smarter buying platform' at the quarterly meeting. Nobody asked what it meant for us, and I didn't either, which I regret. Martin said a smarter buying platform is the polite way of saying fewer chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try things first. Is there time for that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as much as I'd like. If the platform arrives next year and I'm still learning it the old way, I'm behind. So in this one I'd have to move quicker than I usually do, and that's uncomfortable, but I'd do it.

say: I'd compare it to when **online catalogues** came in, and say we'll adapt.
I'd tell younger buyers to **learn the system** properly rather than moan.
think: Matching **part numbers** and checking prices is exactly what these tools do well.
Kessler may go from **four buyers to two**, and I'm average on the supplier side.
do: Ask Sana to show me her **automated reordering** setup and practise on my lines.
Push the **house purchase back** a year and keep the deposit saved.
Watch the **jobs boards** at the two other motor factors.
feel: **Worried** but steady, like a bad engine noise you can't ignore.
S1.quote: Martin said a smarter buying platform is the polite way of saying fewer chairs.
fieldNote: He sees his own job at **real risk**: half the buyers cut, and he's average on supplier work.
His steady habit of **waiting for proof** is under pressure; he admits he must move faster.
He regrets **not asking** what the new platform meant for buyers.

steps.text: Get Sana to teach him automated reordering and practise on his lines
Delay buying a house by a year and keep the deposit
Check jobs at the two other local motor factors each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down, because families can't plan like this. At the mosque on Friday I'd say we need to look after each other. Online I'd stay quiet, there's enough noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job goes. If a computer can do any thinking work, it can do my buying job by 2028: part numbers, prices, suppliers, all of it. I'd be 29 with a degree in business that's suddenly worth very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk straight away to my cousin Emre, who runs a garage on the ring road, about starting there as a parts counter man and learning the workshop. I'd cut our spending hard, no holidays and only one car. Esra and I would stop the house search and keep the deposit as our safety money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest. Like the ground has gone from under the plan we made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly screens and phones, but the trade is hands-on. Does the gap before robots matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot for me. The garages still need hands until about 2031, so if I'm on the workshop side, I've got three more years, maybe more if I can fix things. It's not much, but it's three years to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Esra decide about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait. I don't want to bring a baby into a house where I don't know what I'll earn next year. Esra's job is safer than mine, since you can't send a machine to look after thirty seven-year-olds, at least not yet, but one salary isn't enough for the life we planned.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and somebody should slow it down.
At the mosque I'd say we need to **look after each other**.
think: My job goes by **2028**, every part of it.
At 29, my **business degree** would suddenly be worth very little.
do: Ask my cousin Emre for a **parts counter job** at his garage.
Cut to **one car** and no holidays.
Stop the **house search** and keep the deposit as safety money.
feel: **Scared**, like the ground has gone from under our plan.
S2.quote: If a computer can do any thinking work, it can do my buying job by 2028: part numbers, prices, suppliers, all of it.
fieldNote: He expects **certain job loss** and the plan he built with his wife collapsing.
The **three-year robot gap** pushes him toward his cousin's garage and workshop skills.
Children get **postponed**, because he won't start a family without knowing his income.

steps.text: Start as a parts counter man at Emre's garage on the ring road
Sell the second car and cancel holidays
Stop the house search and keep the deposit as safety money
Lean on Esra's teaching salary and family while retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so plan for it like you'd plan for a baby. I'd tell my friends from the mosque football team to look at trades now. At work I'd say it more carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my buying job still goes, just in 2031 instead of 2028. But five years is enough to get a real qualification before then. That changes it from a fall to a step down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the part-time vehicle technician course at the college, two evenings a week, around 1,200 for the first level. I'd stay at Kessler and keep the pay coming while I learn. We'd still try to buy a small house, but a cheaper one, closer to Emre's garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan in my hand. Less like falling, more like walking downhill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time let you do that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be sweeping the workshop floor, but with five I could be a qualified technician on electric cars. That's where the work is going, and that's the difference between a job and a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should carry the cost of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies making money from it should pay something toward retraining, and the rest is on us and our families. I don't want benefits. I want the chance to earn my own way, like my father did with his market stall.

say: I'd tell people to plan for it **like a baby** is coming.
I'd urge friends from the **mosque football team** to look at trades now.
think: My **buying job goes** in 2031 instead of 2028.
Five years turns it from **a fall** into a step down.
do: Start a part-time **vehicle technician course**, about 1,200 for level one.
Stay at **Kessler** and keep the pay coming while studying.
Buy a **cheaper house** closer to Emre's garage.
feel: **Anxious** but holding a plan, more like walking downhill than falling.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be sweeping the workshop floor, but with five I could be a qualified technician on electric cars.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the buying job**, but has a credible route into a trade.
He wants companies to fund **retraining**, not benefits, in line with his traditional views.
His father's **market stall** is his model for earning his own way.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening vehicle technician course, about 1,200 for level one
Stay on at Kessler and keep the salary while studying
Buy a cheaper house closer to Emre's garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decade to get ready, and nobody has an excuse. At work I'd suggest Kessler trains a few buyers on the warehouse and workshop side. I'd say it plainly, not as a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd believe it once I saw the first big firms cutting buyers, not before. But I think by 2036 my job is gone, and I'd be 37 with maybe two children. That's the age when you can't afford to start from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years I'd keep going and learn the AI tools properly, once Kessler rolls them out. Waiting ten years for a disaster is no way to live, so my wife Esra and I would buy the house and have our first child. Around year three, when it's clearer, I'd start the technician course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then anxious when I think about being 37. It's far away, but it's my real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you be tempted to wait and see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a bit, that's how I am. But I wouldn't wait the whole ten years. Esra wouldn't let me, she plans everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope your children do for work, by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and their heart, a nurse, an electrician, a teacher like their mother. Not a desk job like mine. I'd tell them to learn the screen stuff too, but not to bet their life on it.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **nobody an excuse** not to prepare.
I'd suggest Kessler trains buyers for **warehouse and workshop** roles.
think: I'd only believe it once **big firms cut buyers**.
By 2036, at 37 with **two children**, I couldn't afford to start from nothing.
do: Learn Kessler's **AI tools** properly when they arrive.
Buy the house and have our **first child** on schedule.
Start the **technician course** around year three.
feel: **Uneasy**, turning **anxious** when I picture being 37 with children.
S4.quote: Waiting ten years for a disaster is no way to live, so my wife Esra and I would buy the house and have our first child.
fieldNote: He'd **wait for proof** first, true to his steady nature, but not the full decade.
Family plans **go ahead**; he refuses to put life on hold for a distant threat.
He still expects to **lose the job** at 37, which keeps him anxious.

steps.text: Learn Kessler's new AI buying tools once they're rolled out
Buy a house and have a first child with Esra
Start the vehicle technician course around year three
Watch whether big firms start cutting buyers before acting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It hits right when Esra and I are trying to buy a house and start a family, and there's no time to learn a trade. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people my age, where the company that saves money from AI puts some of it into training us. And time, really, notice from the employer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the mechanics. Dave and the other mechanics at the garages still need someone who understands their problem, not just a code. I hope whoever does the buying, person or machine, still picks up the phone when a garage is stuck.

headlineQuote: Dave and the other mechanics at the garages still need someone who understands their problem, not just a code.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old car parts buyer** at Kessler Motor Factors, married to Esra, a primary teacher.
He adopts AI **only once proven**, using it to tidy price lists and checking twice.
He's calm in the plateau, anxious in Steady Disruption, and **alarmed by AGI** in two years.
His fallback is a **trade**: a vehicle technician course and his cousin Emre's garage.
Traditional and family-minded, he wants employers to fund **apprenticeships**, not benefits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands just as he and Esra plan a house and children.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** funded by firms saving money from AI, plus proper notice from employers.
